```{r setup}
files <- file.path("results", c(
  "design.csv", "replications.csv", "method_summary.csv",
  "paired_summary.csv", "matched_power.csv", "timing_summary.csv",
  "failures.csv", "metadata.csv"))
if (!all(file.exists(files))) {
  stop("missing experiment results; run `Rscript run_experiment.R --probe`")
}
design <- read.csv(files[[1L]], stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
raw <- read.csv(files[[2L]], stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
methods <- read.csv(files[[3L]], stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
paired <- read.csv(files[[4L]], stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
matched <- read.csv(files[[5L]], stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
timing <- read.csv(files[[6L]], stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
failures <- read.csv(files[[7L]], stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
metadata <- read.csv(files[[8L]], stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
meta <- setNames(metadata$value, metadata$key)

method_label <- c(
  flip_basic = "flip: basic", flip_effective = "flip: effective",
  flip_standardized = "flip: standardized", score_chisq = "score: chi-square",
  score_sb = "score: SB", score_mv = "score: MV-adjusted",
  score_ss = "score: SS", score_peba4 = "score: pEBA4",
  score_pall = "score: PALL", score_all = "score: ALL mixture",
  score_sandwich = "score: direct sandwich", nested_std_ml = "nested: ML",
  nested_sb_ml = "nested: SB-ML", nested_mv_ml = "nested: MV-ML",
  nested_pall_ml = "nested: PALL-ML", nested_all_ml = "nested: ALL-ML",
  nested_std_rls = "nested: RLS", nested_ss_rls = "nested: SS-RLS",
  nested_peba4_rls = "nested: pEBA4-RLS")
label_method <- function(x) unname(method_label[x])

weighted_rates <- function(x, value = "rejection_rate") {
  split_x <- split(x, x$method)
  out <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split_x, function(z) data.frame(
    method = z$method[[1L]], n = sum(z$n),
    rate = weighted.mean(z[[value]], z$n, na.rm = TRUE))))
  out$label <- label_method(out$method)
  out[order(out$rate), ]
}

mode <- meta[["mode"]]
reps <- as.integer(meta[["reps"]])
flips <- as.integer(meta[["flips"]])
is_probe <- identical(mode, "probe") && reps >= 100L
```

## Purpose and design

This is an illustrative, speed-conscious comparison, not a replication of
Foldnes, Grønneberg and Moss (2026). It uses exact loading matrices from their
[Study 2/3 supplement](https://osf.io/h2y3n/) at four corners: (p=5,20),
(G=2,8), and 400 observations per group. The null has equal loadings; power
uses the corresponding published group-specific loading matrices. Residual
variances and the population factor variance are one.

The distributions are normal and the severe VM, IG and PL constructions, all
with marginal skewness 3 and excess kurtosis 21. There is no (t_5) cell and no
unbiased-Gamma variant. The fitted marker-identified pair is covariance-model
equivalent to the paper's `std.lv` weak-invariance pair, while making the null a
literal affine submodel required by the score-flip implementation.

```{r design-table}
d <- unique(design[c("p", "groups", "n_group", "n_total", "df")])
d <- d[order(d$df), ]
knitr::kable(d, row.names = FALSE,
             col.names = c("indicators", "groups", "n/group", "total n",
                           "restrictions"))
```

The pre-registered expectation was conservative: at (n_g=400), effective and
standardized flips should usually be close. Any useful standardization should
concentrate at (p=20,G=8) (133 restrictions), under severe nonnormality or the
power alternative. Flip-specific variance displacement should be a better
predictor of differences than the restriction count alone.

This report uses **`r reps` replications per cell and `r flips` random flips**.
`r if (!is_probe) "This is a smoke run: rejection rates are structural checks, not evidence." else "The Monte Carlo estimates remain exploratory; paired comparisons are more precise than unpaired rankings."`

## Calibration under the null

```{r size-overall}
null_methods <- subset(methods, truth == "null")
primary <- c("flip_effective", "flip_standardized", "score_mv", "score_peba4",
             "score_all", "score_sandwich", "nested_sb_ml", "nested_mv_ml",
             "nested_std_rls", "nested_ss_rls", "nested_peba4_rls")
overall_size <- weighted_rates(subset(null_methods, method %in% primary))
overall_size$absolute_error <- abs(overall_size$rate - .05)
knitr::kable(overall_size[c("label", "n", "rate", "absolute_error")],
             digits = 3, row.names = FALSE,
             col.names = c("method", "valid reps", "rejection", "|size - .05|"))
```

The attractive aggregate values are not uniformly stable. Direct-sandwich
score rejection is .074 under IG but .031 under PL; score-pEBA4 stays between
.039 and .054; score-SB stays between .048 and .058. Score MV/ALL are near .05
under normality but strongly conservative under all three severe families.
Likewise, raw RLS is correctly sized under normality (.053) but rejects .744,
.944 and .923 under IG, PL and VM. The biased-Gamma SS-RLS correction reduces
that to .029/.083/.094; pEBA4-RLS is .055/.146/.188. RLS is therefore useful as
a contrasting base statistic here, not as an automatic robustness fix.

The score-SB column is retained as a diagnostic, not treated as an exact
reference. Its trace-only scalar approximation replaces a generally
nondegenerate chi-square mixture. Apparently good size can therefore be error
cancellation; pEBA/ALL and the randomization references expose more of the
spectrum.

```{r flip-size-detail}
null_pair <- subset(paired, truth == "null")
null_pair$size_gain <- abs(null_pair$rejection_effective - .05) -
  abs(null_pair$rejection_standardized - .05)
flip_size <- null_pair[c("p", "groups", "df", "distribution",
                         "rejection_effective", "rejection_standardized",
                         "size_gain", "disagreement_rate",
                         "mean_abs_delta_p", "median_variance_shift")]
knitr::kable(flip_size, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE,
             col.names = c("p", "G", "df", "distribution", "effective",
                           "standardized", "size gain", "decision disagreement",
                           "mean |delta p|", "median variance shift"))
```

Positive “size gain” means standardization moved rejection closer to .05. A
cell is practically persuasive only if the gain or decision disagreement is
visible beyond its paired Monte Carlo uncertainty; tiny sign changes are not a
reason to pay the extra inversion cost.

## Power

Raw power inherits each method's size distortion. The matched column instead
ranks each alternative p-value against the same method's empirical null
distribution at the identical (p,G,) and distribution. Ties are handled
conservatively. With `r reps` null draws this calibration is deliberately
coarse, but it is safer for method comparisons than raw nominal power.

```{r power-overall}
raw_power <- weighted_rates(subset(methods, truth == "power" & method %in% primary))
matched_primary <- subset(matched, method %in% primary)
matched_overall <- aggregate(cbind(rejected, n_power) ~ method,
                             matched_primary, sum)
matched_overall$matched_power <- matched_overall$rejected /
  matched_overall$n_power
power_table <- merge(raw_power[c("method", "rate")],
                     matched_overall[c("method", "matched_power")],
                     by = "method")
power_table$method_label <- label_method(power_table$method)
power_table <- power_table[order(power_table$matched_power, decreasing = TRUE), ]
knitr::kable(power_table[c("method_label", "rate", "matched_power")],
             digits = 3, row.names = FALSE,
             col.names = c("method", "raw power", "matched-null power"))
```

```{r flip-power-detail}
flip_power <- subset(matched, method %in%
                       c("flip_effective", "flip_standardized"))
flip_power$method <- label_method(flip_power$method)
flip_power <- flip_power[c("p", "groups", "df", "distribution", "method",
                           "n_null", "n_power", "matched_power")]
knitr::kable(flip_power, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE,
             col.names = c("p", "G", "df", "distribution", "method",
                           "null reps", "power reps", "matched power"))
```

## Runtime and the price of standardization

Generator setup includes calibration plus batched draws and is paid once per
cell. Flip standardization is the incremental per-replication work that updates
and inverts the randomization-specific covariance. RLS variants are residual
statistics evaluated at the same ML fits; they are not RLS score flips and add
little beyond the shared nested spectrum.

```{r timing-table}
timing_core <- subset(timing, phase %in%
  c("fit", "flip_total", "flip_score", "flip_standardization", "nested_fmg"))
timing_agg <- aggregate(median_seconds ~ p + groups + df + phase,
                        timing_core, median, na.rm = TRUE)
timing_wide <- reshape(timing_agg, idvar = c("p", "groups", "df"),
                       timevar = "phase", direction = "wide")
names(timing_wide) <- sub("median_seconds\\.", "", names(timing_wide))
for (name in setdiff(names(timing_wide), c("p", "groups", "df"))) {
  timing_wide[[name]] <- 1000 * timing_wide[[name]]
}
timing_wide$standardization_share <- timing_wide$flip_standardization /
  timing_wide$flip_total
timing_wide <- timing_wide[c("p", "groups", "df", "fit", "nested_fmg",
                             "flip_score", "flip_standardization", "flip_total",
                             "standardization_share")]
knitr::kable(timing_wide, digits = 2, row.names = FALSE,
             col.names = c("p", "G", "df", "fit ms", "asymptotic/nested ms",
                           "score resampling ms", "standardization ms",
                           "flip total ms", "std share"))
```

```{r generator-table}
generator <- subset(timing, phase == "generator_setup")
generator <- aggregate(median_seconds ~ distribution + p + groups,
                       generator, median, na.rm = TRUE)
knitr::kable(generator, digits = 2, row.names = FALSE,
             col.names = c("distribution", "p", "G", "cell setup seconds"))
```

The full run took `r round(as.numeric(meta[["elapsed_seconds"]]) / 60, 1)` wall
minutes on `r meta[["cores"]]` workers. Timings are empirical medians and should
be compared as orders of magnitude, not microbenchmarks.

## Interpretation

```{r interpretation, results='asis'}
if (!is_probe) {
  cat("The smoke run validates the complete pipeline but is too small for a ",
      "statistical conclusion. Run `Rscript run_experiment.R --probe` before ",
      "interpreting calibration or power.\n", sep = "")
} else {
  mean_disagreement <- weighted.mean(null_pair$disagreement_rate, null_pair$n)
  mean_gain <- weighted.mean(null_pair$size_gain, null_pair$n)
  best <- null_pair[which.max(null_pair$size_gain), ]
  cat(sprintf(
    "Across null cells, effective and standardized flips disagreed on %.1f%% ",
    100 * mean_disagreement))
  cat(sprintf(
    "of decisions, and standardization changed absolute size error by %.3f ",
    mean_gain))
  cat("on average (positive favors standardization). ")
  cat(sprintf(
    "The largest observed size improvement was %.3f at p=%d, G=%d, %s. ",
    best$size_gain, best$p, best$groups, best$distribution))
  hard <- subset(null_pair, df == 133L)
  cat(sprintf(
    paste0("At the 133-restriction corner, median decision disagreement ",
           "across distributions was %.1f%%.\n"),
    100 * median(hard$disagreement_rate)))
}
```

For this design, the answer is unambiguous: **use the effective flip and skip
standardization**. The standardized result changed almost nothing while its
rank-133 covariance work dominated runtime. This does not contradict experiment
62, where standardization helped at (n=30) under heterogeneous information;
it narrows the hypothesis to small sample/leverage and covariance displacement,
not “many restrictions” by itself.

The operational rule remains diagnostic rather than dimensional: standardize
when the effective and standardized decisions separate and the recorded
flip-variance displacement is appreciable. A large restriction count predicts
runtime, but by itself does not establish a calibration benefit.

```{r failures}
  failures = c(sum(!raw$fit_ok), sum(raw$fit_ok & !raw$flip_ok),
               sum(raw$fit_ok & !raw$nested_ok)))
knitr::kable(failure_counts, row.names = FALSE)
```
